https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article.text: Return to Homepage Top Stories: U.S. strikes Iranian tankers Putin meets U.S. envoys Voters' party leanings U.N. adopts new map Starbucks's Snoopy cup Fox News ousts Bartiromo Lindsay Clancy trial Mysterious animal in N.H. 2026 midterms preview 3 hurricanes in the Pacific (Kirill KUDRYAVTSEV/Getty Images) Russia is suspected of launching a series of sabotage operations against European weapons factories in an effort to test NATO's resolve, The Telegraph reported Sunday, citing Western intelligence sources. Russia is recruiting members of local criminal gangs and carefully planning the attacks with "plausible deniability" so they do not reach the threshold that would trigger NATO's Article 5 mutual defense provision. Estonia said Tuesday it was investigating potential Russian involvement in a fire at a building used by defense contractor Milrem Robotics. Bloomberg reported the prosecutor's office suspected arson at the facility used by the manufacturer of autonomous combat vehicles with close ties to Ukraine. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Latvian authorities detained three suspects in connection with the fire and are working with Estonian investigators. State prosecutor Gardi Andersone said investigators were exploring all possible leads, including sabotage, but could not yet share further details. Beyond the Estonian incident, explosions have occurred at facilities operated by major arms manufacturers in Italy and Bulgaria this month alone, according to The Telegraph. Earlier this year, a fire virtually destroyed a Czech plant making drones and thermal optics for Ukraine. Four suspects were detained as part of the investigation into possible Russian involvement. Lithuania also charged six people in connection with an attempt to burn down a factory supplying radio-wave scanners to Kyiv. Advertisement Advertisement On Aug. 10, a major explosion ripped through a plant belonging to EMCO, one of Bulgaria's largest private arms manufacturers of 155 mm artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The incident began when a truck parked near a storage warehouse caught fire, triggering explosions at the facility. Three days later, a similar blast rocked a munitions factory operated by KNDS Ammo Italy in Colleferro on the outskirts of Rome. Italian and Bulgarian officials have sought to play down possible Russian involvement in the incidents, The Telegraph reported, adding that Russia typically leaves little evidence allowing suspected sabotage operations to be directly attributed to Moscow. A Western intelligence assessment previously reported by The Telegraph said Russia's GRU military intelligence agency, known for conducting operations on foreign soil with highly trained agents, had increasingly turned to criminal gangs. Advertisement Advertisement In an interview with The Telegraph in March, Normunds Mežviets, head of Latvia's State Security Service, or VDD, said: "In our experience, we don't see officers of the GRU traveling here physically to our country. "No, they stay in Russia where it's safe," he said. "They're not taking any risks for their own operational and physical security." Instead, GRU officers cultivate sources within criminal gangs that act as intermediaries in targeted countries, communicating through messaging apps such as Telegram. The middlemen then assign tasks to local recruits, who are paid in cryptocurrency and often never learn they are working for Russia. The covert nature of the Kremlin-ordered attacks is seen as a deliberate effort to sow discord among NATO allies, according to The Telegraph. Eastern European members, particularly Poland and the Baltic states, have been far more vocal in accusing Russia of conducting hostile operations across Europe. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved. Photograph: Victorian ombudsman Victoria Boy, 16, held in ‘cramped’ prison cell alone for 22 hours a day for weeks, Victorian ombudsman finds Ombudsman finds government breached teen’s human rights, saying the conditions ‘bordered on solitary confinement’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Benita Kolovos and Bertin Huynh Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 16-year-old boy was held in conditions akin to solitary confinement in adult prison for 22 hours a day, leading him to have suicidal thoughts, a Victorian ombudsman report has revealed. The report, tabled in parliament on Thursday , found the Department of Justice and Community Safety breached the teen’s human rights when transferring him from the Parkville Youth Justice Precinct to the maximum-security Melbourne Assessment Prison in early 2025. The teen was transferred after he attacked staff, following two formal warnings he would be moved to an adult prison if his “violent behaviour” continued. Shackling prisoners giving birth should be a last resort – but it’s happening around Australia anyway Read more When he arrived at the adult prison he was separated from others due to his age, with records showing he spent an average of more than 22 hours in his cell each day for six weeks. The ombudsman, Marlo Baragwanath, said the conditions “bordered on solitary confinement”. The report described the cell as “cramped and worn”, with the boy telling the ombudsman he couldn’t see out of the window. “I was shocked … if you’re in some type of environment like that, I guess you have no hope,” he said. “After a while, it starts playing with your mind.” Even during his outside hours, he was confined to what the ombudsman described as “effectively a room that is open to the sky” and handcuffed due to his history of violence. View image in fullscreen The designated outdoor area at the prison unit. Photograph: Victorian ombudsman He ate his meals in his cell and drank straight from the tap, because a guard wouldn’t provide a cup. “I was like … ‘I’m not a dog,’ you know. [The guard] was like, ‘Huh, you are, mate,’” the teen said. He also had no in-person visits from family for the six weeks, telling the ombudsman he was told he wouldn’t be able to touch them: “If I see them, I want to touch them ‘cause, you know, that’s my family.” The experience led him to suffer “dark, dark thoughts”. “My cell was always dark. I can’t see anything,” he said. “It was playing with my mind. Started thinking stuff I’ve never thought before … a lot of self-harm … Suicidal stuff.” Under Victorian law, a child aged 15 or older can be transferred to an adult prison as a last resort. However, the ombudsman found proper consideration was not given to the child’s human rights in making the transfer application. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “I know many people will find it difficult to sympathise with a child who has been repeatedly violent towards youth justice staff. But human rights apply to everyone, including people accused or convicted of a crime,” Baragwanath said. Tracy Beaton, Victoria’s principal commissioner at the Commission for Children and Young People, said “children’s human rights should never be an afterthought” and welcomed the ombudsman’s eight recommendations, including to ban the transfer of children into adult prisons, though it was rejected by the government. Mindy Sotiri, the executive director of the Justice Reform Initiative, said the report was “indicative of a system that is failing”. “Quite aside from the harm that is caused to children in these circumstances, this approach does absolutely nothing to rehabilitate that child or reduce the risk of them reoffending,” Sotiri said. The Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe said: “Children need love and care and support. When we know that it costs over a million dollars to lock up a child, that money could be better in the wraparound services that actually make a child well.” Victoria’s proposed ‘adult time’ plan to impose life sentences on children condemned by advocates Read more The Victorian Greens justice spokesperson, Katherine Copsey, described the report as an “indictment” of the Labor government, who last year introduced “adult time for violent crime” laws in response to rising youth offending. The Victorian Liberal spokesperson for youth justice, Renee Heath, said Labor was “failing at both ends of the youth justice system” – pointing to an audit released on Wednesday that found there was no evidence the government’s $40m crime prevention program was working. According to the ombudsman, the teen was transferred back to an adult prison after he turned 18 and was no longer separated for safety. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Donald Trump Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office Robert Tait in Washington Sun 27 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 08.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W ith a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing. “All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language. “Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.” Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language. Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second. He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally. A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn. Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025 , when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.) Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April. “President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.” Civility in politics Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies. In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”. View image in fullscreen President Lyndon Johnson meets Richard Nixon at the White House in July 1968. Both men had a taste for the profane. Photograph: National Archives/Getty Images Trump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”. A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard. These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through. Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem. “The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians. “Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.” In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics. Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”. View image in fullscreen JD Vance in Kansas City earlier this month. Photograph: Getty Images Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.” Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity. Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January. Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.” A rhetorical maneuver While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care. “The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.” Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language. “There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them. “It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.” View image in fullscreen Barack Obama with Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa in May. Photograph: Getty Images Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,” suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”. The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses. “I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.” But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.” In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics. “We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands. “Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.” Explore more on these topics Donald Trump US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
